GeometryCirclesCoordinates
Game: Move the yellow points and watch the green line: it always meets the diameter at a right angle.
How to play: Drag T, the centre or the edge point with a mouse or finger, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Press the buttons to show labels, the hint and a check.
Look for the math

Here is a drawing you can pull apart. Take a diameter AB of a circle, two lines from an outside point T that just touch the circle, and join the touch points crosswise to A and B. The point where those two lines meet always sits directly above T. The live cut-the-knot article now shows this figure as a still picture; the original applet, like this page, let you drag the points.

What the picture says

From T, the lines TP and TQ are tangents: each touches the circle at one point. Join A to Q and B to P; they cross at R. Proposition 12 of Archimedes' Book of Lemmas says that the line from T to R meets the diameter AB at a right angle. M is that meeting point.

Put numbers on it

Use coordinates: put the centre at (0, 0), take radius 1, so A = (−1, 0), B = (1, 0) and T = (u, v) with u² + v² > 1. A point on the circle can be written with one number t as ((1−t²)/(1+t²), 2t/(1+t²)). The tangent at it has equation x·X + y·Y = 1, so making T lie on that line gives

(u + 1)t² − 2v·t + (1 − u) = 0.

The two roots t₁ and t₂ belong to P and Q. Their product is (1−u)/(1+u), and that is all we need.

Where R lands

For the point with parameter t, the slope of the line from A is exactly t and the slope of the line from B is exactly −1/t. At x = u the two lines have the same height precisely because t₁·t₂ = (1−u)/(1+u). So

R = (u, v ± √(u² + v² − 1)).

R and T have the same x-coordinate: the line TR is upright while AB lies flat, which is the proposition. The logic test confirms this on thousands of arrangements, with T above, below and to either side of the circle.

Why the lengths match

The height difference between R and T is √(u² + v² − 1), the same as the tangent length TP. That is the power of the point T: TP² = TO² − r². Hence TP = TQ = TR, and O = 2T − P (P reflected in T) lies on that same circle, which is what the Hint button draws. The page's remark adds that M, P, T and Q are concyclic. A second proof joins AP and BQ at a point that is the triangle's orthocenter, making TR an altitude and the right angle immediate.

Try putting T almost on the circle or directly above the centre: R shoots far away, but the line through T and R still points straight at the diameter.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
